question: If you cut the first instant off a recorded note, what happens to listeners' ability to name the instrument?
answer: It drops sharply. The French composer Pierre Schaeffer cut the attack, the first instant of a note, from tape recordings, and listeners struggled to tell instruments apart. Levitin uses the experiment to show that timbre, an instrument's sound colour, depends heavily on how a note begins.
move: The first instant of a sound tells us most about its source.
trap: 'Nothing changes': the rest of the note sounds just the same.
simply: A violin and a trumpet can play the same note. Your ear tells them apart mostly from the first split second, when the sound starts.
why: It explains why the start of a voice, a word or a song carries so much, and why sound engineers fuss over how notes begin.

book.title: This Is Your Brain on Music
book.author: Daniel J. Levitin
